lesson.title: Driving the Speaker: The Power Amplifier
lesson.summary: A power amplifier is the final stage in an audio signal chain, built to deliver real electrical power into a low-impedance loudspeaker rather than simply raising a voltage, converting a small, well-shaped line-level signal into the watts needed to physically move a speaker cone.
lesson.body:
Earlier stages, the audio amplifier and the preamplifier, are built to raise voltage while drawing very little current. A loudspeaker, typically 4 to 8 ohms, is a demanding low-impedance load that needs real current, not just voltage swing, to move air and produce sound. The small-signal op-amps and transistors used in earlier stages generally cannot source or sink anywhere near enough current for this. Power amplifiers use higher-current output devices specifically built to deliver both voltage swing and current into that low impedance at the same time.

Suppose a power amp produces a 4V rms sine wave across an 8 ohm speaker. Delivered power is P = V squared divided by R = (4V)^2 / 8 ohm = 16 / 8 = 2W.

Now suppose the input power to this power amp stage is 2mW and the output power measured at the speaker is 2W, a power ratio of 2W / 0.002W = 1000. Because this is a power ratio rather than a voltage ratio, the power form of the decibel applies: 10 times log10(1000) = 10 times 3 = 30dB of power gain.

Whatever power a power amplifier draws from its supply beyond what it actually delivers to the speaker has to go somewhere, and it leaves as heat. That is why power amp output stages, unlike the small-signal stages earlier in this chain, are typically built with heatsinks and given explicit attention to thermal design, a concern that voltage-only stages like the preamp rarely need to worry about.
